big: Meena earns ₹60,000 a month and cannot explain where it goes. By the 20th the account is nearly empty. She is not careless. She just has never looked at the full picture.

lines: I do not buy anything big. So why am I always short?
Usually because of many small things. Let us sort every rupee into piles and see.

alt: A bar split into fixed costs, variable costs and savings
caps: Fixed costs are the same every month: rent, EMI, school fees, insurance.
Variable costs move: food, travel, orders, shopping. This is where the money hides.
Once she tracked it, 11% of the pay moved from variable spending into savings.
Her savings rate went from about 4% to 15%. Same salary, clearer picture.

alt: Bars growing as the number of ₹250 orders in a month rises
caps: Ten orders in a month is ₹2,500.
Twenty-five orders is ₹6,250, which is more than many people's monthly SIP.
Small and frequent is how variable spending hides.

q: Meena saved ₹9,000 out of her ₹60,000 take-home pay. What is her savings rate?
opts: 15%, since savings divided by take-home pay is 9,000 over 60,000
9%, since that is the rupee amount divided by 1,000 in each case
30%, since savings are compared with her fixed costs only
6.7%, since the saving is divided by the amount she spent
why: Savings rate is saved money divided by take-home pay. Nine thousand over sixty thousand is 15%.
Rupee amounts are not a rate. A savings rate compares savings with what she takes home.
Fixed costs are not the base. The rate is measured against all the pay she receives.
The base is take-home pay, not spending. Dividing by spending gives a different, misleading figure.

q: Rohan wants to find money to save. His fixed costs are ₹30,000 and his variable spending is ₹25,000. Where is the easier saving?
opts: In the fixed pile, since it is the largest part of his spending each month
In neither, since both piles are essential to his daily life
In the variable pile, where small trims add up without big changes
In the fixed pile, since rent can be renegotiated every month
why: Fixed costs are hard to change quickly. They are the harder place to find savings.
Variable spending includes wants, so some of it can be trimmed. Not all of it is essential.
Variable costs move month to month, and small trims add up without changing his life much.
Rent is fixed for a term and cannot be renegotiated every month, so it is slow to change.

q: Dadi owns a house worth ₹50 lakh and a savings of ₹5 lakh, and owes ₹10 lakh on a loan. What is her net worth?
opts: ₹55 lakh, which is everything she owns added together
₹45 lakh, which is what she owns minus what she owes
₹10 lakh, which is the loan that she has to repay
₹5 lakh, which is the cash that she has at hand
why: Adding assets ignores what she owes. Net worth subtracts the debts from what she owns.
Net worth is assets minus debts: ₹55 lakh owned minus ₹10 lakh owed gives ₹45 lakh.
The loan is a debt, so it is subtracted from what she owns, not used as her net worth.
Cash is only part of what she owns. Net worth counts all assets and all debts.

q: Rohan tracks his spending for a month and finds ₹4,000 of food orders he did not notice. What is the best next step?
opts: Ignore it, since a single month of data cannot prove anything useful at all
Cancel every food app for good and never order food again, from any place
Stop tracking, since looking at it only makes him feel worse
Set a monthly limit, so the spending is a choice and not a habit
why: A month of data is enough to show a pattern. Ignoring it wastes the point of tracking.
A total ban rarely lasts. A limit he can keep works better than a rule he will break.
Tracking is what exposes the leaks. Stopping removes the information he needs to improve.
A limit turns unnoticed spending into a choice he makes on purpose, without banning it entirely.

pts: Sort spending into fixed and variable. Variable is where small leaks hide.
Savings rate is what you saved divided by your take-home pay.
Net worth is what you own minus what you owe. Check it twice a year.
